title: From Polling to Events: Building a Reactive MQL5 Trading System with Python and Redis Streams
text:
Introduction
An Expert Advisor can poll an external service for signals, and at low volume nothing feels wrong. A timer, an HTTP request, and a list of pending actions are enough, and the code is easy to follow.
The trouble starts when the system has to survive a crash, a retry, or a broker reply that is neither a clear yes nor a clear no. Was this signal already handled? Did that order reach the broker before the restart? Should this message ever be read again?
This article follows that problem from a simple polling loop to a small prototype built on Redis Streams. MQL5 publishes market events, Python turns them into trading ideas, and the EA decides what happens next. The EA still polls on a timer. What changes is not the mechanism, but the semantics: every message gets a stable identity, an explicit acknowledgment, and a way out when it cannot be used.
One rule runs through the design. Python is allowed to suggest a trade. It is not allowed to place one. The final decision always stays inside MQL5.
When polling stops being simple
In its simplest form, OnTimer() calls WebRequest() on a Python endpoint every few seconds, and the EA tries an order for every signal returned. With one producer, one consumer, and at most one signal per bar, this works. The real problem appears one crash later.
Messages can be processed twice: if the EA crashes after sending an order but before recording it, the signal comes back looking brand new. Without an acknowledgment, "finished" and "never seen" look the same. Invalid records can get stuck: a message the EA cannot parse returns on every poll. And broker outcomes are rarely binary: a loop that only knows "filled" retries a partial fill that already traded, and retries a margin rejection forever.
None of this is caused by polling itself. Polling works when the protocol behind it is explicit: stable IDs, acknowledgments, a rejection path, and processing that gives the same result when it runs twice. Part of that comes ready-made from Redis Streams. The rest has to be built in the EA.
Redis Streams help, but only with delivery
A Redis stream is an append-only log. Producers add entries with XADD, and every entry gets a transport ID such as 1792622276177-0. Consumers read through a consumer group, which keeps a pending entries list (PEL): an entry handed to a consumer stays pending until the consumer confirms it with XACK, and after a restart the consumer reads its own pending entries again with XREADGROUP and ID 0, and new ones with ID >.
That sounds minor, but it changes the whole failure model. A crash no longer loses a message, and a message can no longer disappear quietly: every entry is either acknowledged, still pending, or explicitly moved somewhere else.
The wrapper uses only the commands it needs. Creating the group comes first:
# ensure_group - create a consumer group if it does not exist
    def ensure_group(self, stream_name: str, group_name: str) -> None:
        """Create a consumer group if it does not already exist.

        A new group starts at '$': it receives only messages published after
        it was created, so a newly started EA does not replay the whole stream
        history (those signals would be stale anyway).

        Only BUSYGROUP (the group already exists) is ignored. Any other Redis
        error, such as WRONGTYPE when the key is not a stream, is logged and
        raised to the caller.
        """
        try:
            self.redis.xgroup_create(stream_name,                             # target stream
                                     group_name,                              # group name
                                     id='$',                                  # only messages after creation
                                     mkstream=True)                           # create stream if absent
        except redis.exceptions.ResponseError as e:
            if str(e).startswith('BUSYGROUP'):                                # group already exists?
                return                                                        # expected: nothing to do
            logging.error(f'XGROUP CREATE {group_name} on {stream_name} failed: {e}') # unexpected Redis error
            raise                                                             # let the caller decide
XGROUP CREATE fails with BUSYGROUP when the group already exists, which is normal on every restart, so only that error is ignored. Anything else, such as WRONGTYPE, is logged and raised; hiding it would leave an EA that silently receives nothing. A new group starts at $, so an EA does not replay old signals, and the strategy must start before the EA, or its group misses the first bars.
Reading new entries has a trap of its own:
# consume_new_events - fetch never-delivered messages
    def consume_new_events(self, stream_name: str,                            # source stream
                           group_name: str,                                   # consumer group
                           consumer_name: str,                                # consumer instance
                           count: int = 10,                                   # max messages
                           block_ms: Optional[int] = None                     # None = never block
                           ) -> List[Tuple[str, Dict]]:
        """Return messages that have never been delivered to this consumer group.

        block_ms=None  -> no BLOCK argument: the call returns immediately.
        block_ms=N > 0 -> wait at most N milliseconds for new messages.
        BLOCK 0 is deliberately never sent: in Redis it means "wait forever".
        """
        if block_ms is not None and block_ms <= 0:                            # refuse an unbounded wait
            raise ValueError('block_ms must be None or a positive number of milliseconds') # BLOCK 0 = wait forever
        self.ensure_group(stream_name, group_name)                            # group must exist
        response = self.redis.xreadgroup(group_name,                          # consumer group
                                         consumer_name,                       # consumer name
                                         {stream_name: '>'},                  # never-delivered only
                                         count=count,                         # max messages
                                         block=block_ms)                      # None = do not block
        return self._flatten(response)                                        # return the list
In Redis, BLOCK 0 does not mean "do not wait". It means "wait forever". The gateway is single-threaded, so one blocked read would stall every request, including the EA's publication of the very bar that would produce the awaited signal. The wrapper therefore never sends it.
So far, so good. But delivery is only half of the story.
XACK tells Redis that an entry no longer needs to stay pending. It does not tell us whether an order was sent, accepted, or filled before a restart. Treat an ACK as proof of execution, and the first crash in the wrong place produces a duplicate trade. To close that gap, the EA needs three things of its own: a durable journal that recognizes a redelivered signal even after a restart, a link from every order and deal back to its signal, and a decision for every broker reply: accepted, worth retrying, or final.
Why MQL5 keeps the final say
Business correctness starts with a question of authority. A signal carries a direction and a reference to its bar, but no volume, no price, and no stop levels, and nothing in it can switch a check off. Every check that decides whether an order is valid, safe, and sendable runs inside the EA, in ExecutionGuard.
Why be this strict? Because the boundary has to hold even when Python is wrong. A strategy bug, a misconfigured deployment, or a local process writing to Redis can do no more than a correct signal could. The worst a bad signal can do is what the guard would allow a good one to do. Note what this promises: every order conforms to the EA's rules, not that the trade is a good idea.
A signal that fails any check in Table 1 is rejected, journaled, and acknowledged.

Table 1. What the guard checks, and why.
Normalization clamps the configured volume into the broker's range and rounds it down to whole volume steps, taking the decimals from the step itself, so 0.125 keeps three. A final check in NormalizeVolume() rejects anything still invalid. A stricter risk policy could refuse an out-of-range volume instead of clamping it. After the guard, OrderCheck() validates margin and the full request.
Python keeps only the soft decision. Here an up bar means BUY and anything else SELL. The confidence of 0.8 in the signal is decorative: nothing reads it.
The age check needs one clock. TimeCurrent() is server time, Python's time.time() is local time, and the two differ by the broker's time-zone offset. So the EA stamps BAR_CLOSED with TimeCurrent(), the strategy copies it unchanged into source_event_time, and the guard measures on that same clock:

This measures the age of the market data, so any delay in Python, Redis, or the gateway counts against the signal. That is deliberate: a decision based on old data is stale, however recently it was computed. Python's event_time and Redis stream IDs play no part in freshness.
The event model
The guard can only check what an event carries, and acknowledgments need a stable envelope:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Enum: ENUM_EVENT_TYPE - all event categories in the system       |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
enum
ENUM_EVENT_TYPE
  {
   EVENT_BAR_CLOSED       =
0
,
// a chart bar has closed
EVENT_SIGNAL_GENERATED =
1
,
// Python has produced a trading signal
EVENT_ORDER_ATTEMPTED  =
2
,
// the EA is about to send an order
EVENT_DEAL_EXECUTED    =
3
,
// the broker has filled a deal
EVENT_POSITION_UPDATED =
4
// an open position has changed
};
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Struct: EventEnvelope - compact container for one event          |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
struct
EventEnvelope
  {
string
event_id;
// application-level unique identifier
string
stream_id;
// Redis transport ID (empty when publishing)
ENUM_EVENT_TYPE   event_type;
// category of this event
string
source;
// module that produced this event
datetime
event_time;
// creation timestamp (Unix seconds)
string
symbol;
// trading symbol related to this event
string
payload;
// JSON string carrying extra fields
};
The event_id is the logical identity: what the event is about. The stream_id is where Redis stored this copy. They sit next to each other on purpose, because mixing them up is the classic mistake. A redelivery keeps the stream_id; a republished copy gets a new one but keeps its event_id. Deduplication uses the event_id, acknowledgment the stream_id, never the other way around.
Field
Gateway check
event_id, source, symbol, event_type
Required text; event_type must be known; a missing event_id is never replaced by the Redis ID
event_time
Positive integer (Unix seconds); for signals, audit data only
payload
A flat JSON object; values are finite numbers or text without quotes, backslashes, braces, or control characters; booleans, null, arrays, and nested objects are refused
Table 2. Envelope fields and gateway checks.
The payload rules look fussy, and they exist for one reason. The EA parses JSON with a small, constrained parser, so the gateway refuses anything it cannot read instead of repairing it. A boolean is valid JSON, but the parser does not handle it, so it is refused before it is stored. Inside the EA the payload is a JSON string that the serializer maps to and from the object on the wire.
Every event_id is built from durable facts, never from a counter (Table 3), so the same bar announced twice gives the same signal ID and the journal recognizes it. Redis does not deduplicate; the EA does, per signal.
Event
Producer and stream
event_id

BAR_CLOSED

bar_time, open, high, low, close, tick_volume

Table 3. Event types, identities, and payloads.
ORDER_ATTEMPTED records what the EA decided to submit; DEAL_EXECUTED records what the broker executed. One attempt can produce no deal, or several partial ones.
The strategy enforces the BAR_CLOSED payload in validate_bar_event() instead of trusting it:
# validate_bar_event - check required fields and the complete OHLC bar
def validate_bar_event(event: dict) -> bool:
    """Check that the event is a valid BAR_CLOSED with a complete, consistent OHLC bar.

    open, high, low, and close are all required, must be finite and positive,
    and the high-low range must contain both the open and the close.
    """
    if event.get('event_type') != 'BAR_CLOSED':                   # must be the right type
        return False                                              # reject wrong events
    if not event.get('event_id'):                                 # must have an ID
        return False                                              # reject missing ID
    if not event.get('symbol'):                                   # must have a symbol
        return False                                              # reject missing symbol
    try:                                                          # must have an integer timestamp
        if int(event.get('event_time')) <= 0:                     # positive Unix seconds (server clock)
            return False                                          # reject non-positive time
    except (TypeError, ValueError):                               # missing or non-numeric
        return False                                              # reject missing time

    # decode the payload and require all four prices
    try:
        payload = json.loads(event.get('payload', '{}'))          # decode payload JSON
        bar = {k: float(payload[k]) for k in ('open', 'high', 'low', 'close')} # all four required
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, TypeError, ValueError): # malformed or missing price
        return False                                              # reject incomplete payload

    # reject NaN, Infinity, zero, and negative prices
    if not all(math.isfinite(p) and p > 0 for p in bar.values()): # float('nan') does not raise
        return False                                              # reject invalid numbers

    # OHLC consistency: the high-low range must contain the open and the close
    if bar['high'] < max(bar['open'], bar['close']):              # high below the body?
        return False                                              # reject inconsistent bar
    if bar['low'] > min(bar['open'], bar['close']):               # low above the body?
        return False                                              # reject inconsistent bar
    return True                                                   # event is valid
All four prices must be finite, positive, and consistent. The isfinite() check matters because float("nan") does not raise. An invalid bar is acknowledged and discarded; a failed publication of the signal leaves the bar pending for a retry.
From market event to trade attempt
The EA publishes BAR_CLOSED through the gateway. The strategy, which talks only to Redis, publishes SIGNAL_GENERATED. On each timer tick the EA fetches pending and new signals, filters duplicates through its journal, runs the guard and OrderCheck(), publishes ORDER_ATTEMPTED, and calls OrderSend(). Deals arrive later as DEAL_EXECUTED (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Reactive event flow from market event to confirmed trade.
The MQL5 side is timer-driven, and that is not a stylistic choice: MQL5 has neither a Redis client nor an asynchronous HTTP client. Figure 2 shows how each event crosses the stream boundaries.
Figure 2. Event lifecycle across stream boundaries.
One bar, end to end
This cycle comes from the demo test described later. At 17:03:00 an M1 bar of EURUSD# closed and the EA published BAR_CLOSED. The strategy published a SELL signal with the bar's server time and acknowledged the bar; the EA never acknowledges BAR_CLOSED, since it only publishes it. About a second later the EA received the signal, found no journal entry, passed the guard and OrderCheck(), published ORDER_ATTEMPTED, wrote ATTEMPTING, and sent the order. The broker answered 10009 (DONE); the EA journaled ACCEPTED with the ticket and acknowledged the signal in its own group, mql5-EURUSD_-123456, where "#" became "_" because group names travel in a URL.
17:03:00.305  Published BAR_CLOSED event: BAR_CLOSED:EURUSD#:M1:1792602120
17:03:01.281  OrderCheck passed for SIGNAL:BAR_CLOSED:EURUSD#:M1:1792602120:simple-1: retcode=0 (Done)
17:03:01.997  Order accepted: EURUSD#, volume=0.1, type=SELL, order=999271786, retcode=10009
17:03:02.069  Published DEAL_EXECUTED: DEAL_EXECUTED:1187726132 (signal SIGNAL:BAR_CLOSED:EURUSD#:M1:1792602120:simple-1)
Figure 3. Event identity across the round trip.
The link from deal to signal rests on ordering. The EA writes result.order into the journal before OnTimer() returns, and trade transactions arrive only after that, so OnTradeTransaction() finds the signal through DEAL_ORDER. A partial fill produces several DEAL_EXECUTED events with the same IDs. The order comment carries a second link, an 11-character tag: RS- plus the FNV-1a hash of the signal ID, which lets the EA find its order after a restart even before any deal. The signal is acknowledged on the OrderSend() result, not on the first deal, because the ACK answers "did this become an accepted order?", not "what was executed?".
Reading and acknowledging signals
The gateway is the only component that speaks both HTTP and Redis. It exposes /publish, /consume, /ack, and /reject, and contains no trading logic. This is how it answers a poll:
# handle_consume - return pending and new events for a consumer
    def handle_consume(self):
        """Return up to `count` events: pending entries first, then new ones.

        New entries are only requested for the remaining capacity, so the
        gateway never claims messages it does not return. Neither read
        blocks. Records that violate the contract are dead-lettered and
        acknowledged here instead of being returned.
        """
        # parse query parameters from the URL
        params   = parse_qs(urlparse(self.path).query)                        # parse query string
        stream   = params.get('stream',   ['signal.events'])[0]               # stream name
        group    = params.get('group',    [CONSUMER_GROUP])[0]                # group name
        consumer = params.get('consumer', [CONSUMER_NAME])[0]                 # consumer name
        try:
            count = max(1, min(int(params.get('count', ['10'])[0]), MAX_COUNT)) # bounded batch size
        except ValueError:                                                    # non-numeric count?
            self.send_json(400, {'error': 'count must be an integer'})        # bad request
            return                                                            # abort handling

        try:
            # recover messages already assigned to this consumer
            pending = redis_stream.consume_pending_events(stream, group, consumer, count=count) # XREADGROUP 0

            # fetch never-delivered messages only for the remaining capacity
            remaining = count - len(pending)                                  # free slots in this response
            new = redis_stream.consume_new_events(stream, group, consumer,
                                                  count=remaining) if remaining > 0 else [] # XREADGROUP >

            # validate each record; dead-letter the ones that break the contract
            result = []                                                       # response accumulator
            for msg_id, record in pending + new:                              # pending first, then new
                envelope, error = normalize_envelope(record)                  # validate and normalize
                if error:                                                     # poison message?
                    reject_record(stream, group, msg_id, record, error)       # dead-letter and ACK
                    continue                                                  # do not return it
                result.append({'stream_id': msg_id, **envelope})              # transport ID emitted first

            # return the compact JSON array to the caller
            self.send_json(200, result)                                       # success
        except Exception as e:                                                # catch any error
            logging.error(f'Consume error: {e}')                              # log server-side
            self.send_json(500, {'error': str(e)})                            # server error
Pending entries come first, and new ones fill only the remaining capacity, so the gateway never claims an entry it does not return. The same normalize_envelope() check runs on publication, where a violation gets HTTP 400, and here, where a bad record is copied to signal.events.dlq with its reason and acknowledged. The value check is short:
# parser_safe - True if a value can be read by the MQL5 parser
def parser_safe(value):
    """Strings must not contain quotes, backslashes, braces, or control characters;
    numbers must be finite. Booleans, nested objects, arrays, and null are not allowed."""
    if isinstance(value, bool):                                               # true / false?
        return False                                                          # not in the contract; checked first because a bool is also an int
    if isinstance(value, (int, float)):                                       # numeric value
        return math.isfinite(value)                                           # NaN and Infinity are not JSON
    if isinstance(value, str):                                                # text value
        return not any(c in UNSAFE_CHARS or ord(c) < 32 for c in value)       # no breaking characters
    return False                                                              # dict, list, None
The bool test comes first because in Python a bool is also an int. If a record still fails to parse in the EA, its stream_id goes to /reject, and the gateway dead-letters and acknowledges it. That second line of defense was never needed in the tests.
Acknowledging is where an earlier version trusted too much. The gateway returns HTTP 200 whenever it handled the request, but XACK reports how many entries it removed, and zero means the entry was not pending: already acknowledged, or a wrong group or ID. Redis does not say which. So the EA counts an ACK only when the reply says "acknowledged":true:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Acknowledged - did XACK actually remove the entry?               |
//| HTTP 200 only means that the gateway answered. XACK returns 0    |
//| both for an entry that was already acknowledged and for a wrong  |
//| group or ID, so "acknowledged":false never counts as success.    |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+

""

(

// acknowledgment confirmed
}

"entry was not pending (already acknowledged, or wrong group or ID)"

}

//| AckEvent - acknowledge a processed event via Redis stream ID     |

An unconfirmed ACK leaves the entry pending; it returns on the next poll and the journal recognizes it. It costs a round trip, never a second order.
One more line came from testing:
# send_json - write a JSON response with a status code
    def send_json(self, status, body):
        """Serialize body as compact JSON and send it with the given status."""
        data = json.dumps(body, separators=COMPACT).encode('utf-8')           # compact UTF-8 body
        self.send_response(status)                                            # status line
        self.send_header('Content-Type', 'application/json')                  # JSON content
        self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(data)))                    # body length
        self.send_header('Connection', 'close')                               # new connection per request; MT5 under Wine fails on reuse
        self.end_headers()                                                    # finish headers
        self.wfile.write(data)                                                # write body
Python's HTTPServer closes the connection after every reply. MetaTrader 5 under Wine appeared to reuse it, so every second request failed with error 1003 before reaching the gateway. Connection: close fixes that.
Surviving restarts: the journal and reconciliation
Redis remembers what is pending, not what the EA already did. That memory is SignalJournal, an append-only file per symbol and magic number, where every transition is flushed before the EA acts on it:

const

// entry to persist

//--- open the file for appending (created if absent)

h =

MarkAttempting(), MarkAccepted(), and MarkRejected() all go through Transition(), which updates memory only if Append() succeeded and returns that result. Each line reads event_id|state|updated|attempts|order. On start-up, entries older than a day are dropped; if the journal cannot be loaded, OnInit() fails and the EA refuses to trade.
State
Written when
On redelivery
ATTEMPTING (1)
After ORDER_ATTEMPTED, before OrderSend()
Reconcile with the broker first
ACCEPTED (2)
The broker accepted; the ticket is stored
Acknowledge only; not proof of a fill
REJECTED (3)

A signal for another symbol is acknowledged only in this EA's group, because every EA reads every signal in its own group; two EAs on one symbol therefore need different magic numbers. The TestStopAfterOrderSend block is a test switch, off by default, that stops the EA right after an accepted OrderSend() so a crash can be reproduced.
The window between OrderSend() and the journal
ATTEMPTING marks an attempt whose result was never recorded: the EA stopped just before or just after OrderSend(), or the reply was ambiguous, such as TIMEOUT or CONNECTION. A deal is no proof either way, since a PLACED order may not have filled. On redelivery, ReconcileAttempt() searches active orders, then the order history, for this signal's tag, magic number, and symbol. Some brokers replace order comments, so an order without any tag is matched by its setup time; an order with another signal's tag never matches. There are three answers:
RECONCILE_FOUND: the order exists and was not rejected, so the signal becomes ACCEPTED and is never resent;
RECONCILE_NONE: the history is trustworthy and empty, so the signal goes through the guard again, freshness included;
RECONCILE_UNKNOWN: the terminal is disconnected or HistorySelect() failed, so the signal waits; guessing "no order" would cause a duplicate.
This is still a heuristic, and the last section says where it can fail.

OrderCheck() must both succeed and report a success code. The documentation does not name that code, so the EA accepts 0 or DONE and logs it; the demo run returned 0. A failed check is classified like an OrderSend() retcode but never counts as accepted, and it happens before anything is recorded.
ORDER_ATTEMPTED is fail-closed: if the gateway does not confirm it, no order is sent. An audit trail with gaps could not be trusted to show what the EA sent. Then ATTEMPTING is written, the price refreshed, and the order sent. ClassifyRetcode() sorts the reply:

//| ClassifyRetcode - transient vs permanent broker outcomes         |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
ENUM_EXEC_OUTCOME ClassifyRetcode(
const
uint
retcode)
// trade server return code
{
switch
(retcode)
// dispatch on the return code
{
case
TRADE_RETCODE_DONE
:
// full fill
case
TRADE_RETCODE_DONE_PARTIAL
:
// partial fill
case
TRADE_RETCODE_PLACED
:
// order accepted, fill pending
return
(EXEC_ACCEPTED);
// final: ACK
case
TRADE_RETCODE_REQUOTE
:
// price moved
case
TRADE_RETCODE_PRICE_CHANGED
:
// price moved
case
TRADE_RETCODE_PRICE_OFF
:
// no quotes right now
case
TRADE_RETCODE_TOO_MANY_REQUESTS
:
// throttled
case
TRADE_RETCODE_LOCKED
:
// request locked for processing
case
TRADE_RETCODE_FROZEN
:
// order or position frozen
case
TRADE_RETCODE_TIMEOUT
:
// outcome unknown: reconciled on the next pass
case
TRADE_RETCODE_CONNECTION
:
// outcome unknown: reconciled on the next pass
case
TRADE_RETCODE_MARKET_CLOSED
:
// session closed: retried until the signal is stale
return
(EXEC_TRANSIENT_FAILURE);
// leave pending
default
:
// NO_MONEY, INVALID_VOLUME, INVALID_PRICE,
return
(EXEC_PERMANENT_FAILURE);
// TRADE_DISABLED, INVALID_STOPS, REJECT, 0, ...
}
  }
DONE, DONE_PARTIAL, and PLACED are accepted: accepted by the broker, not necessarily filled, and while a PLACED order is active the guard blocks new entries. Price and load errors are retried; TIMEOUT and CONNECTION stay pending and are reconciled before any resend.
MARKET_CLOSED is transient, because a closed session is a temporary condition: the signal is retried until it is older than MaxSignalAgeSeconds, then rejected as stale, so a signal from a closed session is dropped after a minute, not executed at the reopen. Everything else, such as NO_MONEY, is final. The same age limit bounds every retry, which is why one day of journal history is plenty.
Setting up the environment
By now the design is complete on paper. Running it is short work, but the order in which the components start matters more than any version. Redis must be 5.0 or later, where consumer groups appeared; redis-cli ping should answer PONG. Python needs one package, installed with pip install redis. In MetaTrader 5, add http://127.0.0.1:8000 under Tools > Options > Expert Advisors > Allow WebRequest for listed URL, and switch Algo Trading on.
Then start python gateway.py, which prints "Gateway running on port 8000", and python strategy_consumer.py, before attaching the EA, because the strategy's group starts at $ and would miss earlier bars. Finally, redis-cli XINFO GROUPS signal.events should list mql5-{symbol}-{magic}, and XINFO GROUPS market.events the group strategy.
My own first run still failed, for a configuration reason: plain EURUSD was not tradeable on the demo account, and the guard said so in the log until the EA moved to EURUSD#.

for: The guard checks 'Age on the trade-server clock between zero and MaxSignalAgeSeconds' — a concrete, quantifiable time-based filter tied to signal freshness
The age check uses 'source_event_time' stamped by TimeCurrent() on BAR_CLOSED and measured against current TimeCurrent(), enabling exact second-level delta calculation on historical data
MaxSignalAgeSeconds is a configurable input (default 60), explicitly described as 'a deliberate constraint' and 'bounds every retry', making it a testable parameter
The rule 'a decision based on old market data is stale' directly links age filtering to trading logic correctness, implying that violating it degrades performance
The journal drops entries older than a day, but the active filter is MaxSignalAgeSeconds (60s), which governs real-time eligibility — this threshold is both defined and bounded in the text

non_fatal: Статья не содержит ни торгового правила (условия входа), ни рыночного признака/фильтра: вся статья посвящена архитектуре распределённой системы событий (Redis Streams, MQL5-Python взаимодействие), инфраструктуре доставки сигналов, надёжности, журналированию и обработке сбоев — но не описывает, *как формируется сам сигнал* (например, по ценам, объёмам, индикаторам).

Отсутствует описание модели или логики генерации сигнала в Python: упоминается лишь «up bar means BUY and anything else SELL» — это тривиальное эвристическое правило без точной формулы (неясно, как определяется «up bar»: по close>open? по close>open предыдущего бара? требуется ли фильтрация спреда/тиков? нет указания на таймфрейм, способ сравнения, обработка незакрытого бара), и оно не приведено как рабочее правило или признак для XGBoost.

Нет описания признаков, вычисляемых из цен/спреда/объёмов/времени: все упомянутые данные (open/high/low/close/tick_volume) передаются как сырые поля BAR_CLOSED-события, но *никакая их комбинация, преобразование или нормализация не описана как входной признак* — например, нет RSI, MA, ATR, spread-to-ATR, volume delta, time-since-last-bar и т.п.
Указано, что «confidence of 0.8 in the signal is decorative: nothing reads it» — подтверждает отсутствие используемой количественной метрики или признака.

Все проверки в ExecutionGuard (spread, age, symbol state и др.) — это фильтры *валидации*, а не *генерации сигнала*: они разрешают/запрещают сделку *после* получения сигнала, но не являются рыночными признаками, вычисляемыми из цен/объёмов и пригодными как Feature_Or_Filter.

judge.summary: Статья описывает архитектурное решение для надёжной доставки торговых сигналов между Python и MQL5 через Redis Streams, включая механизмы дедупликации, журналирования, подтверждения и восстановления после сбоев.
